screens.title: Legacy Input Manager vs Input System
screens.narratorSegment: Unity historically provided the Legacy Input Manager with named axes like Horizontal and Vertical that return floats between minus one and one. This is simple, reliable, and built into every Unity project, which makes it perfect for short prototypes and for learners. The newer Input System package offers action maps, device abstraction, and event-driven input which is better for larger, multi-device projects. For this chapter we deliberately use the Legacy Input Manager so you can focus on how to treat input values rather than learn an additional system. A practical example: Input. GetAxis("Horizontal") returns a smoothly interpolated value based on key press or joystick movement; you multiply that value by moveSpeed and by Time. deltaTime to get stable movement. A common misconception is that the newer system is always better; the right tool depends on project complexity. If you only need simple keyboard movement, the legacy axes keep code concise and reduce setup. As a reflective question, consider whether your game will require multiple control schemes or complex rebinding — if so, plan to switch to the Input System later.

Legacy Input Manager
Built-in axes, minimal setup, ideal for keyboard movement and simple controllers.
How it works
  • Axes defined in Project Settings produce values from -1 to 1.
  • Call Input.GetAxis("Horizontal") to read smooth input values.
  • Good for WASD, arrows, and simple gamepad sticks.
Example: Input.GetAxis("Horizontal") * moveSpeed * Time.deltaTime for frame-independent movement.
Misconception: newer is not always required. For a single control scheme, the legacy manager is simpler and faster to iterate with.
Input System (overview)
Action maps and device independence for larger projects and rebinding support.
When to use
  • Multiple devices and action maps.
  • Need for rebinding and event-driven callbacks.
  • Recommended for complex, cross-platform titles.
Practical tip: Start with Legacy to learn physics, then migrate only if your project needs advanced input features.

screens.title: What is a Rigidbody?
screens.narratorSegment: A Rigidbody is a Unity component that hands control of an object’s translation and rotation to the physics engine. When you add a Rigidbody, the object responds to gravity, collides with other physics objects, and reacts to forces. This is different from moving the Transform directly, which bypasses collision resolution and can cause clipping or teleportation. For example, translating transform. position every frame may push the player through walls because physics is not asked to resolve the movement. With Rigidbody movement, you either set its velocity or apply forces like AddForce so the physics engine computes collisions and responses. A common misconception is that physics always makes things slower; in fact, physics provides consistent collision response and helps avoid subtle bugs during interactions. In practice, choose Rigidbody-based movement when your player must push objects, be affected by gravity, or collide naturally. If you only need purely cinematic motion with no collisions, transform updates are acceptable. The practical rule: if you want realistic interactions, use a Rigidbody and work within FixedUpdate. What is a Rigidbody? means use rigidbody when you need gravity, collisions, or force-driven responses; avoid changing transform directly for physics objects.. In practical terms, why a rigidbody gives your gameobject gravity, collisions, and realistic motion. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Rigidbody
Rigidbody: the physics controller
Gives an object mass, gravity, collision response, and the ability to receive forces.
Why not transform changes?
Directly setting transform.position bypasses the physics engine and can cause tunneling through colliders or unpredictable collisions.
Example: set rb.velocity = new Vector3(x * speed, rb.velocity.y, z * speed) to move while preserving gravity on the Y axis.
Common mistake: applying Rigidbody forces in Update rather than FixedUpdate can lead to jitter because physics updates run on a fixed timestep.
Concrete analogy
Think of Rigidbody as handing the object to the physics clerk so all collisions and gravity are processed on the physics schedule.
Key Takeaway

Rigidbody enables realistic motion and collision; prefer physics-based methods over transform updates for interactive objects.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Basic Movement
Movement pattern
Sample input, create direction, apply to Rigidbody while keeping gravity intact.
// Read axes in Update, apply in FixedUpdate
void Update()
{
  float moveHorizontal = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
  float moveVertical = Input.GetAxis("Vertical");
  movement = new Vector3(moveHorizontal, 0f, moveVertical);
}

void FixedUpdate()
{
  rb.velocity = new Vector3(movement.x * moveSpeed, rb.velocity.y, movement.z * moveSpeed);
}
Explanation
  • GetAxis smooths input and supports negative values for opposite directions.
  • Storing input in Update avoids missed frames; applying in FixedUpdate matches physics timing.
  • Preserve rb.velocity.y so gravity keeps working naturally.
Common mistake: calling AddForce without Time.fixedDeltaTime then using Update to apply forces; always prefer FixedUpdate for physics and scale by fixedDeltaTime when appropriate.
Key Takeaway

Sample input in Update, apply motion to Rigidbody in FixedUpdate; expose moveSpeed for tuning.

screens.title: Physics Timing: Update vs FixedUpdate
screens.narratorSegment: Unity has two update loops that are important for movement: Update and FixedUpdate. Update runs every rendered frame and is the right place to read input because it captures user actions with as little latency as possible. FixedUpdate runs on a fixed timestep and is the right place to modify Rigidbody state because physics calculations run at consistent intervals. The practical pattern is: read axes and button presses in Update, store those values, and then use them inside FixedUpdate to set velocity or call AddForce. An example: if you read jump input in Update, you still check it and call rb. AddForce inside FixedUpdate or call AddForce directly from Update but using flags to ensure physics happens at fixed steps. A common pitfall is applying physics in Update which can introduce jitter or inconsistent forces on different machines. Another point: use Time. deltaTime for frame-tied calculations and Time. fixedDeltaTime within FixedUpdate if you multiply by a time factor. The core insight is separating capture from application so input remains responsive and physics remains stable. In practical terms, why sampling input and applying physics on different update loops matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Update vs FixedUpdate
Step sequence
A reproducible process to capture input and apply physics safely.
1. Capture input
Read axes and buttons in Update for minimal latency.
2. Store state
Keep movement and jump flags in member variables for use in physics step.
3. Apply physics
Use FixedUpdate to set velocity or call AddForce so physics resolves reliably.
Example
Read Input.GetButtonDown("Jump") in Update to capture the press, set a flag, and then in FixedUpdate call rb.AddForce(Vector3.up * jumpForce, ForceMode.Impulse) if the flag and grounded check are true.
Pitfall: applying movement directly in Update can cause inconsistent collision responses and jitter across different frame rates.
Key Takeaway

Separate capture and physics: Update for input, FixedUpdate for Rigidbody changes, and use the matching time delta for time-based scaling.

AddForce(Vector3. up * jumpForce, ForceMode. Impulse). ForceMode. Impulse tells the physics engine to apply the force as a single immediate change in velocity, which is perfect for a jump that should feel instant. Crucially, you must prevent repeated jumps while airborne. The common solution is to check whether the player is grounded before applying the impulse; a grounded boolean can be computed using a Physics. CheckSphere at a GroundCheck transform or using collision/trigger events with a ground LayerMask. For example, only call AddForce when Input. GetButtonDown("Jump") returns true and isGrounded is true. A frequent misconception is that you should repeatedly apply a small upward force while the jump button is held; that creates floaty movement. Instead, use a single impulse and optionally allow a small fall modifier or coyote time for polish. The result is a crisp jump that still respects gravity and collisions. Implementing jump
Apply an instantaneous upward impulse and guard it with a grounded check.
// In Update
if (Input.GetButtonDown("Jump") && isGrounded)
{
  rb.AddForce(Vector3.up * jumpForce, ForceMode.Impulse);
}
Design note: consider adding coyote time or a small double-jump window if you want more forgiving controls, but keep the base jump an impulse for predictable physics.
Ground check example
Use Physics.CheckSphere(groundCheck.position, radius, groundLayer) to set isGrounded and prevent the jump when false.

screens.title: Ground Checking Techniques
screens.narratorSegment: Detecting whether a character is grounded is essential to prevent infinite jumping and to enable grounded-only actions. One simple method is Physics. CheckSphere using a small radius at a GroundCheck transform placed near the player’s feet. CheckSphere returns true when it touches colliders in the ground layer, which you specify with a LayerMask. Another method is a downward raycast that tests for distance to the ground; raycasts can be more precise if the player has non-spherical feet or varying terrain. Collision callbacks are also useful: when OnCollisionEnter reports a contact with the ground layer, set grounded true, and set it false on OnCollisionExit. Whichever method you choose, keep the check lightweight and consistent with your Rigidbody size. A typical pitfall is a too-large radius or an incorrect LayerMask, which makes the character appear grounded while slightly above the floor. For robust behavior, visualize the check in the editor with Gizmos so you can see the sphere or ray during development. Finally, ensure your ground objects are assigned to the correct ground layer before testing. Ground Checking Techniques means use checksphere, raycast, or collision events with a specific ground layermask and small radius to reliably detect grounded state.. In practical terms, checksphere, raycasts, and collision layers for reliable grounded detection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: AddForce vs Setting Velocity
screens.narratorSegment: There are two common approaches to move a Rigidbody: applying AddForce and directly setting rb. velocity. AddForce applies acceleration which interacts with mass and other forces, making it appropriate when you want physically simulated acceleration, such as pushing objects or simulating momentum. Setting rb. velocity replaces the current velocity directly, giving tight, arcade-style control that is simpler to author for character controllers. For example, setting rb. velocity = new Vector3(x * speed, rb. velocity. y, z * speed) produces immediate, deterministic movement that ignores accumulated forces on the horizontal axes. A common misconception is that AddForce is always more realistic. While it can be, it also requires careful tuning of mass, drag, and the force magnitude to achieve responsive control. If your goal is crisp player movement that resists sliding, directly setting velocity is often simpler. If you need interactions like being pushed by explosions or realistic friction, AddForce combined with appropriate drag and mass yields more emergent behavior. Choose the method that matches the movement style you want. Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Hands-on Activity
Starter script preview
Copy this into PlayerMovement.cs, attach to Player, and assign GroundCheck and Ground layer.
using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerMovement : MonoBehaviour
{
  public float moveSpeed = 5f;
  public float jumpForce = 8f;
  public Transform groundCheck;
  public LayerMask groundLayer;

  private Rigidbody rb;
  private bool isGrounded;
  private Vector3 movement;

  void Start()
  {
    rb = GetComponent<Rigidbody>();
    if (rb == null)
    {
      Debug.LogError("Rigidbody not found on Player! Please add one.");
      enabled = false;
    }
  }

  void Update()
  {
    isGrounded = Physics.CheckSphere(groundCheck.position, 0.2f, groundLayer);

    if (Input.GetButtonDown("Jump") && isGrounded)
    {
      rb.AddForce(Vector3.up * jumpForce, ForceMode.Impulse);
    }
  }

  void FixedUpdate()
  {
    float moveHorizontal = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
    float moveVertical = Input.GetAxis("Vertical");
    movement = new Vector3(moveHorizontal, 0f, moveVertical);
    movement = transform.TransformDirection(movement);

    rb.velocity = new Vector3(movement.x * moveSpeed, rb.velocity.y, movement.z * moveSpeed);
  }
}
Editor configuration
Set moveSpeed to 5, jumpForce to 8, and create a Ground layer assigned to your Plane.
Create GroundCheck child at Y = -0.5 relative to Player and link to the script.
Test: use WASD and Spacebar; if sliding increase Rigidbody Drag.
Polish: consider interpolation on Rigidbody for smoother visuals and coyote time for better jump feel.
Key Takeaway

Follow the build-test-tune loop: code the script, configure the scene, reproduce issues, and iterate with Inspector values until movement feels correct.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll learn how player input becomes character motion. You will see why using a Rigidbody matters, how Unity’s Legacy Input Manager exposes axes like Horizontal and Vertical, and how to keep movement stable across different frame rates. We’ll start with the simple input model because it’s built into Unity, then show how to apply movement with physics so collisions and gravity behave predictably. A short, concrete example: reading Input. GetAxis gives you a float between minus one and one, which you multiply by a move speed and a time factor to make movement frame-rate independent. We’ll also cover jumping as an instant impulse and how to prevent infinite mid-air jumps by checking whether the player is grounded. Finally, you’ll learn common fixes for sliding, jittery motion, and why physics updates belong in FixedUpdate while input checks belong in Update. By the end, you’ll be able to create a controllable character that feels solid and responds to keyboard controls without clipping or teleporting. What movement quality will you aim for first: responsiveness or realism?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to tell the difference between Unity’s Legacy Input Manager and the newer Input System, and implement keyboard movement using C# and Rigidbody-based physics. You will learn to apply forces and set velocity on a Rigidbody to achieve responsive movement while preserving collisions. You’ll practice checking whether the player is grounded so jumps act only when appropriate. Finally, you will be able to diagnose typical movement bugs like sliding, teleporting, or jitter and fix them using Rigidbody properties and correct update methods. Each objective includes a concrete example and a verification milestone so you can test competence in the Editor. These are practical, inspector-friendly skills: you will expose moveSpeed and jumpForce to iterate quickly and confirm behavior in Play mode. The focus is on predictable physics first, then polish. Which objective will you try first when you open Unity?

This second objectives page shows how to practice and verify those four skills in the Unity Editor. For the input system objective, open Project Settings and inspect the Horizontal and Vertical axes to see how they map to keys. To practice movement you will create a Player GameObject, add a Rigidbody, and expose moveSpeed and jumpForce as public fields so you can tune feel in Play mode. For physics interactions, the exercise asks you to move the Rigidbody with AddForce or by setting velocity in FixedUpdate and observe collisions with environment objects. For troubleshooting, run the scene and reproduce sliding or infinite jumping; then change Rigidbody Drag or add a grounded check to confirm the fix. Each verification milestone is simple: observe a player that stops predictably when input ceases, cannot jump while airborne, and uses gravity naturally. These practices bridge knowledge and applied skill so you can iterate quickly while preserving physics correctness.

Unity historically provided the Legacy Input Manager with named axes like Horizontal and Vertical that return floats between minus one and one. This is simple, reliable, and built into every Unity project, which makes it perfect for short prototypes and for learners. The newer Input System package offers action maps, device abstraction, and event-driven input which is better for larger, multi-device projects. For this chapter we deliberately use the Legacy Input Manager so you can focus on how to treat input values rather than learn an additional system. A practical example: Input. GetAxis("Horizontal") returns a smoothly interpolated value based on key press or joystick movement; you multiply that value by moveSpeed and by Time. deltaTime to get stable movement. A common misconception is that the newer system is always better; the right tool depends on project complexity. If you only need simple keyboard movement, the legacy axes keep code concise and reduce setup. As a reflective question, consider whether your game will require multiple control schemes or complex rebinding — if so, plan to switch to the Input System later.

A Rigidbody is a Unity component that hands control of an object’s translation and rotation to the physics engine. When you add a Rigidbody, the object responds to gravity, collides with other physics objects, and reacts to forces. This is different from moving the Transform directly, which bypasses collision resolution and can cause clipping or teleportation. For example, translating transform. position every frame may push the player through walls because physics is not asked to resolve the movement. With Rigidbody movement, you either set its velocity or apply forces like AddForce so the physics engine computes collisions and responses. A common misconception is that physics always makes things slower; in fact, physics provides consistent collision response and helps avoid subtle bugs during interactions. In practice, choose Rigidbody-based movement when your player must push objects, be affected by gravity, or collide naturally. If you only need purely cinematic motion with no collisions, transform updates are acceptable. The practical rule: if you want realistic interactions, use a Rigidbody and work within FixedUpdate. What is a Rigidbody? means use rigidbody when you need gravity, collisions, or force-driven responses; avoid changing transform directly for physics objects.. In practical terms, why a rigidbody gives your gameobject gravity, collisions, and realistic motion. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

To create basic movement you read the Horizontal and Vertical axes, build a movement vector, and apply it to the Rigidbody. Input. GetAxis returns a float between minus one and one which represents direction and pressure on a stick or a key state. Multiply this value by a configurable moveSpeed and the appropriate time factor. In character physics we prefer to use Time. fixedDeltaTime when applying forces or making velocity changes inside FixedUpdate, but when assembling input values you often sample them in Update and store them for the next FixedUpdate. A concrete pattern: read Input. GetAxis in Update, compute a Vector3 movement, then in FixedUpdate set rb. velocity = new Vector3(movement. x * moveSpeed, rb. velocity. y, movement. z * moveSpeed). This preserves existing vertical velocity so gravity still works. A common misconception is to multiply by Time. deltaTime in FixedUpdate; you should use Time. fixedDeltaTime inside physics updates when time scaling is needed. Try exposing moveSpeed so you can tune responsiveness from the Inspector. How would changing moveSpeed affect player control and feel? In practical terms, from input.getaxis to a movement vector you can apply to a rigidbody. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Unity has two update loops that are important for movement: Update and FixedUpdate. Update runs every rendered frame and is the right place to read input because it captures user actions with as little latency as possible. FixedUpdate runs on a fixed timestep and is the right place to modify Rigidbody state because physics calculations run at consistent intervals. The practical pattern is: read axes and button presses in Update, store those values, and then use them inside FixedUpdate to set velocity or call AddForce. An example: if you read jump input in Update, you still check it and call rb. AddForce inside FixedUpdate or call AddForce directly from Update but using flags to ensure physics happens at fixed steps. A common pitfall is applying physics in Update which can introduce jitter or inconsistent forces on different machines. Another point: use Time. deltaTime for frame-tied calculations and Time. fixedDeltaTime within FixedUpdate if you multiply by a time factor. The core insight is separating capture from application so input remains responsive and physics remains stable. Physics Timing: Update vs FixedUpdate means read input in update for responsiveness; apply motion and forces in fixedupdate to keep physics stable and deterministic.. In practical terms, why sampling input and applying physics on different update loops matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A jump is typically modeled as an instantaneous upward impulse applied to a Rigidbody. In Unity that is commonly implemented with rb. AddForce(Vector3. up * jumpForce, ForceMode. Impulse). ForceMode. Impulse tells the physics engine to apply the force as a single immediate change in velocity, which is perfect for a jump that should feel instant. Crucially, you must prevent repeated jumps while airborne. The common solution is to check whether the player is grounded before applying the impulse; a grounded boolean can be computed using a Physics. CheckSphere at a GroundCheck transform or using collision/trigger events with a ground LayerMask. For example, only call AddForce when Input. GetButtonDown("Jump") returns true and isGrounded is true. A frequent misconception is that you should repeatedly apply a small upward force while the jump button is held; that creates floaty movement. Instead, use a single impulse and optionally allow a small fall modifier or coyote time for polish. The result is a crisp jump that still respects gravity and collisions. Jump Mechanics and ForceMode.Impulse means use forcemode.impulse for immediate jumps and gate the impulse with a grounded check to prevent infinite mid-air jumping.. There are two common approaches to move a Rigidbody: applying AddForce and directly setting rb. velocity. AddForce applies acceleration which interacts with mass and other forces, making it appropriate when you want physically simulated acceleration, such as pushing objects or simulating momentum. Setting rb. velocity replaces the current velocity directly, giving tight, arcade-style control that is simpler to author for character controllers. For example, setting rb. velocity = new Vector3(x * speed, rb. velocity. y, z * speed) produces immediate, deterministic movement that ignores accumulated forces on the horizontal axes. A common misconception is that AddForce is always more realistic. While it can be, it also requires careful tuning of mass, drag, and the force magnitude to achieve responsive control. If your goal is crisp player movement that resists sliding, directly setting velocity is often simpler. If you need interactions like being pushed by explosions or realistic friction, AddForce combined with appropriate drag and mass yields more emergent behavior. Choose the method that matches the movement style you want.
